paper.title: Danish parents’ vaccination readiness is associated with their children’s officially registered vaccination history
paper.code_data_availability: “The study materials, synthetic survey data (with simulated demographic variables), and analysis code are available via the Open Science Framework (OSF; …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish registry data on children’s vaccination (official vaccination registry data)
variables_mentioned: seasonal influenza dose in the autumn/winter 2021/2022 season

registers.name_in_paper: register data on parents’ COVID-19 vaccination status

registers.role: sample frame (initial screening of eligible parents) and definitions of citizenship and immigration status

linkages: Parents’ survey responses matched to their child’s official vaccination registry data via Denmark’s registry numbers (93.2 % of consenting parents, n = 2740)
Parents’ own COVID-19 vaccination status checked against register data
Eligible parents identified by an initial screening via Statistics Denmark and invited via Denmark’s official digital post (e-Boks)

sample.universe: People with a permanent address in Denmark who were a parent of a child up to five years old as on August 10th, 2020
sample.unit_of_observation: Parent (survey respondent) matched to one child; in the three-vaccine analysis the unit is a parent×vaccine observation (up to three per participant)
selection_rules: Permanent address in Denmark and parent of a child up to five years old as on August 10th, 2020
Sampling accounted for parent’s gender, age, region of residence, educational level, citizenship status, number of people and number of children in the household, aiming at a representative sample
Initial screening via Statistics Denmark resulted in 12,277 people invited via Denmark’s official digital post
2941 parents consented and answered the survey (full survey sample)
93.2 % of them (n = 2740) could be matched to a child in a meaningful way via Denmark’s registry numbers (matched sample)
Matched sample used whenever officially recorded (registry) data on children’s vaccination were analysed; full survey sample used in the second and last analysis steps
sample.period: Influenza uptake refers to the autumn/winter 2021/2022 season; ethics approval dated 22.08.2022; the survey field period is not stated
sample.n_observations: 7,880 parent×vaccine observations in the three-vaccine models; 2,740 observations in the influenza models
sample.n_individuals: 2,941 consenting parents; 2,740 matched to a child

construction_notes: For each of the four childhood vaccines the number of doses the child received was divided by the number of doses they were eligible for; values equaling one indicated complete (1 = complete; incomplete otherwise)
The questions on vaccination were adjusted according to the child’s age; registry vaccination status was used instead of survey proxies
In the case of influenza, having received a dose in the autumn/winter 2021/2022 season was considered as complete

DiTeKiPol-Hib, PCV and MMR uptake analysed jointly (up to three observations per participant) because these vaccines are part of the program and had similar uptake levels; influenza analysed separately because it is offered seasonally and had much lower uptake

7C vaccination readiness scale (long version for parents): 7-point Likert items averaged for the overall scale or sub-scales; for the overall score negatively framed items were recoded, while calculation, complacency, conspiracy and constraints were kept un-recoded when entered as separate factors
Trust items: four sources (public news media, private news media, the government’s official websites, social media) on a 7-point Likert scale
Certainty about the child’s next vaccination measured on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = very uncertain, 5 = completely certain)

Education coded 1 (baseline) = primary/secondary/vocational education, 2 = short cycle and vocational bachelor’s education, 3 = bachelor and master programs in Table 3; Figures 1 and 2 use a finer six-category education coding with primary school as baseline
Regions coded 1 (baseline) = Capital region, 2 = Midtjylland, 3 = Nordjylland, 4 = Sjælland, 5 = Syddanmark
To avoid separation problems, Danish and Danish descendant parents were considered in the same group (baseline) in Table 3
All analyses conducted in R version 4.3.0

links.pointer_quote: More precisely, a one-point increase in parents’ vaccination readiness score was associated with a two-fold increase in the likelihood of the child being vaccinated with the three main vaccines in the program.

More precisely, a one-point increase in parents’ vaccination readiness score was associated with a two-fold increase in the likelihood of the child being vaccinated with the three main vaccines in the program.

claims.statement: In Table 3, Model 1A, Parents’ vaccination readiness (overall 7C score) is positively associated with completion of all eligible doses of the three regular childhood vaccines (DiTeKiPol-Hib, PCV, MMR) (OR = 2.34).

treatment.label: Parents’ vaccination readiness (overall 7C score)

register_source.value: Survey of parents (not register data); panel-provider survey linked to Danish registry data via Denmark’s registry numbers

definition.value: Overall score of the long version of the 7C Vaccination Readiness Scale for parents (Rees et al. [23]); items answered on a 7-point Likert scale from 1 = fully disagree to 7 = fully agree, the score obtained by averaging the responses for the overall scale, with negatively framed items recoded so that each factor indicates a positive association with vaccination readiness. Entered as a continuous predictor; the coefficient is the odds ratio for a one-unit increase.

timing.value: Measured in the survey, cross-sectionally with respect to the registered vaccination history

outcome.label: Completion of all eligible doses of the three regular childhood vaccines (DiTeKiPol-Hib, PCV, MMR)

register_source.value: Danish vaccination registry data on children’s vaccination, matched to the survey via Denmark’s registry numbers (the paper names no register code)

definition.value: For each of the four childhood vaccines the number of doses the child received was divided by the number of doses they were eligible for; values equaling one indicated complete (1 = complete; incomplete otherwise). Uptake of DiTeKiPol-Hib, PCV and MMR was analysed jointly, giving up to three observations in the response variable per participant (one per vaccine).

timing.value: Child’s officially registered vaccination history at the time of the study (children aged 0–5 years)

units.value: odds ratio for a one-unit increase in the predictor

magnitude.interpretation: a two-fold increase in the likelihood of the child being vaccinated with the three main vaccines in the program

estimand.target_population: Parents in the matched sample (n = 2740): parents residing in Denmark with a child up to five years old who consented to the survey and could be matched to a child via Denmark’s registry numbers

population.description: Parents with a permanent address in Denmark and a child up to five years old as on August 10th, 2020, who consented to the survey and could be matched to a child via Denmark’s registry numbers (n = 2740)
population.ages: Children 0–5 years; parents aged 18–29, 30–39 and 40+ years (mean 35.2 years, SD 5.7)
population.period: Registry vaccination history of children aged 0–5; influenza uptake refers to the autumn/winter 2021/2022 season (survey field date not stated)
population.selection: An initial screening via Statistics Denmark resulted in 12,277 people invited via Denmark’s official digital post; 2941 parents consented and answered the survey, of which 93.2 % (n = 2740) could be matched to a child in a meaningful way via Denmark’s registry numbers

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation between surveyed parents; no reform, lottery, discontinuity or other exogenous variation is used. Survey measures are linked to officially registered vaccination histories.

key_assumptions.assumption: The officially registered vaccination history in the Danish registry data measures the child’s actual vaccine uptake
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 2.3.4 states that the official vaccination status was used instead of survey proxies; the Limitations concede potential deficient information from the registry data, e.g. for children of immigrant parents

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysed sample is conditioned on consenting to the survey and on being matched to a child via Denmark’s registry numbers
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 2.2 reports the 93.2 % match rate and states that the resulting sample was not perfectly representative with regards to gender and education

key_assumptions.assumption: The self-reported 7C vaccination readiness scale (and the trust and certainty items) measure the intended psychological constructs
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reports high internal consistency of the scale (McDonald’s ω = 0.91) and reliability per sub-scale in Table 2

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimates are cross-sectional associations: the design exploits no exogenous variation in the predictor, so a causal reading would require that no unmeasured common cause of the predictor and the child’s vaccination status is present
Observations are clustered by participant (up to three vaccine observations per parent) and cluster robust standard errors with participant as cluster account for that dependence
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 2.4.1 and in the note to Table 3

threats_discussed: Potential deficient information from the registry data — some vaccinations of children of immigrant parents may not have been captured in the registry at the time of the study
Using a binary completion variable per vaccine (and not per dose) may mean only the most relevant variables stood out as significant
The sample was not perfectly representative with regards to gender and education
robustness_checks: Models 2A and 2B re-estimate the association adding parent’s age group, gender, educational level, region, citizenship status, COVID-19 vaccination status and child’s age group as predictors
Registry vaccination status used instead of the survey proxies (Supplemental File 2, Table S1 compares the two)

estimator.value: logistic regression (coefficients reported as odds ratios)

estimation.specification: Logistic regression of completion of all eligible doses (1 = complete) on parents’ vaccination readiness and vaccine class, estimated jointly over DiTeKiPol-Hib, PCV and MMR with up to three observations per participant
estimation.clustering: cluster robust standard errors with participant as cluster

source_table.value: Table 3, Model 1A

heterogeneity.dimension: vaccine (three regular childhood vaccines vs. seasonal influenza)
heterogeneity.finding: The same one-unit increase in vaccination readiness is associated with a smaller odds ratio for the seasonal influenza vaccine (Model 1B) than for the three regular childhood vaccines (Model 1A)

population.ages: Children 0–5 years; parents aged 18–29, 30–39 and 40+ years (mean 35.2 years, SD 5.7)
population.period: Registry vaccination history of children aged 0–5; influenza uptake refers to the autumn/winter 2021/2022 season (survey field date not stated)
population.selection: An initial screening via Statistics Denmark resulted in 12,277 people invited via Denmark’s official digital post; 2941 parents consented and answered the survey, of which 93.2 % (n = 2740) could be matched to a child in a meaningful way via Denmark’s registry numbers

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation between surveyed parents; no reform, lottery, discontinuity or other exogenous variation is used. Survey measures are linked to officially registered vaccination histories.

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysed sample is conditioned on consenting to the survey and on being matched to a child via Denmark’s registry numbers
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 2.2 reports the 93.2 % match rate and states that the resulting sample was not perfectly representative with regards to gender and education

key_assumptions.assumption: The self-reported 7C vaccination readiness scale (and the trust and certainty items) measure the intended psychological constructs
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reports high internal consistency of the scale (McDonald’s ω = 0.91) and reliability per sub-scale in Table 2

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimates are cross-sectional associations: the design exploits no exogenous variation in the predictor, so a causal reading would require that no unmeasured common cause of the predictor and the child’s vaccination status is present

threats_discussed: Potential deficient information from the registry data — some vaccinations of children of immigrant parents may not have been captured in the registry at the time of the study
Using a binary completion variable per vaccine (and not per dose) may mean only the most relevant variables stood out as significant
The sample was not perfectly representative with regards to gender and education
robustness_checks: Models 2A and 2B re-estimate the association adding parent’s age group, gender, educational level, region, citizenship status, COVID-19 vaccination status and child’s age group as predictors

population.selection: An initial screening via Statistics Denmark resulted in 12,277 people invited via Denmark’s official digital post; 2941 parents consented and answered the survey, of which 93.2 % (n = 2740) could be matched to a child in a meaningful way via Denmark’s registry numbers

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-sectional variation between surveyed parents; no reform, lottery, discontinuity or other exogenous variation is used. Survey measures are linked to officially registered vaccination histories.

key_assumptions.assumption: The analysed sample is conditioned on consenting to the survey and on being matched to a child via Denmark’s registry numbers
key_assumptions.supported_by: Section 2.2 reports the 93.2 % match rate and states that the resulting sample was not perfectly representative with regards to gender and education

key_assumptions.assumption: The self-reported 7C vaccination readiness scale (and the trust and certainty items) measure the intended psychological constructs
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper reports high internal consistency of the scale (McDonald’s ω = 0.91) and reliability per sub-scale in Table 2

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimates are cross-sectional associations: the design exploits no exogenous variation in the predictor, so a causal reading would require that no unmeasured common cause of the predictor and the child’s vaccination status is present

threats_discussed: Potential deficient information from the registry data — some vaccinations of children of immigrant parents may not have been captured in the registry at the time of the study
Using a binary completion variable per vaccine (and not per dose) may mean only the most relevant variables stood out as significant
The sample was not perfectly representative with regards to gender and education
robustness_checks: Models 2A and 2B re-estimate the association adding parent’s age group, gender, educational level, region, citizenship status, COVID-19 vaccination status and child’s age group as predictors
Registry vaccination status used instead of the survey proxies (Supplemental File 2, Table S1 compares the two)

estimator.value: linear regression (OLS) with robust standard errors

estimation.specification: Separate linear regression models with demographics as independent variables and each of the 7C factors and trust items as dependent variables; estimates displayed in Figures 1 and 2 (Tables S7-S8, Supplemental File 2)

source_table.value: Figure 1 (coefficient plot); direction stated in the running text, Section 3.2

ambiguities: No numeric estimate is printed: Figures 1 and 2 are coefficient plots and the text states only the direction, so point estimate, interval and p-value are left null.
Statistical significance is recorded as true because the paper reports the association as a finding; the article prints no p-value for this coefficient.
The prose statement summarises several dummy coefficients plotted in the figure (one per category), so this claim is not tied to a single printed coefficient.

evidence.annotation: Note. Baseline categories: parent’s age group = 18–29 years; education = primary school; gender = female; region = capital region; parent’s citizenship = Danish. R2collective r. = 0.022, R2confidence = 0.045, R2compliance = 0.028, R2calculation = 0.020, R2complacency = 0.022, R2constraints = 0.024, R2conspiracy = 0.134. N = 2941. Horizontal bars indicate 95 % confidence intervals using robust standard errors.
